In the early 19th century, a Welsh textile manufacturer named Robert Owen decided that all the world's problems were caused by religion. Specifically, it was his position that newborn humans were simply gobs of clay, and who they turned out to be, their 'character' was entirely dependent on outside factors. This was at odds with the widely accepted Calvinism of the period, which suggested that there is something static and steadfast in each human being that will make its way to the surface as maturity grows, regardless of externals.

He began publishing his ideas in 1813, and in 1816 set out to prove his ideas by creating the Institute for the Formation of Character at New Lanark, Scotland. The core of this institution was a science-based secular curriculum, with a heavy emphasis on each student striving to improve/enrich the lives of his fellow students. This was supposed to churn out happy little socialists. I don't actually know how that turned out.

In 1825, he came to the United States to ply his theories here, and established a colony at New Harmony, IN. It failed after two years. After rigorous analysis of the failure, Owen and his disciples ("Owenites") arrived that the conclusion that in order for such a society to function, a government run education program the instills Owen's ideas from an early age must come first, and that would create little socialists that go on to form communes. She edited and published (with Owen's help) the Free Inquirer, a radical socialist newsletter.

As they toured the United States on speaking circuits, their anti-Biblical ideas repelled quite a few people from Owenism. But the more immediate work was to get out system of schools adopted. To this end, it was proposed to organize the whole Union secretly, very much on the plan of the Carbonari of Europe, of whom at the time I knew nothing.

The members of this secret society were to avail themselves of all means in their power, each in his own locality, to form public opinion in favor of education by the State at the public's expense, and to get such men elected to the legislature as would be likely to favor our purposes.
